Most of what you need is already sitting in your files. You just never connect it.

Anthropic engineers put out a graph engineering blueprint that turns those dead folders - papers, project notes, meeting transcripts, buried decisions - into a second brain that Claude is able to query.

The pipeline goes documents → entities → relationships → graph → retrieval → an answer with its sources.

Six moves:

1. Extract - pull out people, projects, tools and events, and tag every relationship with a source ID and evidence so it traces back.
2. Resolve - treat "Sensor-X" and "Sensor X" as possibly one thing: merge what's confirmed, flag what's unsure, keep real differences apart.
3. Connect - record each actor, its action, the target and the file it came from, so you follow links across files instead of stitching them by hand.
4. Profile - choose a project, person or tool and build a grounded profile from its excerpts and the facts around it, with conflicts left visible.
5. Retrieve - go from an affected component to the incident to its reviewer, merge facts from several documents and cite each source.
6. Check - give Claude Code the prompt below plus a goal and your documents. Begin with a single folder, review what got extracted, then widen.

Building a research assistant or an AI second brain? Keep this workflow next to your next build.

Bookmark it, then dig into the complete guide, "Context, Harness, Loops, Prompts" ↓

virals.name: Aakash Gupta
virals.text:
A Christmas market in England advertised itself with an AI picture of a cozy wooden lodge, fairy lights everywhere, and a stage set up for a band. One vendor paid £180 for a stall.

Opening day was a concrete warehouse with about five stalls and a red bucket on the floor catching rain from the roof.

Entry was free, so the money came from vendors like her. And the way they got pulled in is kind of clever.

Think about how a new market gets off the ground. Vendors won't pay for a spot unless they believe crowds are coming, and crowds won't come unless there are vendors worth seeing. Every market has to break that loop somehow, and the honest way takes years of showing up and building a reputation.

This one used a picture. The same image went out to vendors and shoppers, and each side looked at it and saw the other side already there. Vendors say they were promised 50-plus stalls and 2,500-plus visitors a day.

The guy who made the images, David Rowland, runs the bigger Winter Wonderland attraction next door. He called it a "lesson learned" and said you're never going to get it looking exactly like the picture. The organizers have since cancelled every booking and promised full refunds.

Glasgow pulled the same move in February 2024. Willy's Chocolate Experience sold £35 tickets off AI posters so sloppy they had made-up words on them, families walked into a mostly empty warehouse, and somebody called the cops. Nearly three years later, the pictures look a whole lot more real.

So is this legal? Nope, and it hasn't been for a long time. Britain passed the Trade Descriptions Act back in 1968. The UK ad watchdog says AI images get judged the same as photos. And since April 2025, the competition regulator can fine a company up to 10% of its global revenue without even going to court. One vendor is already talking to lawyers.

Faking a place used to be expensive, though. Fyre Festival paid Kendall Jenner $250,000 for one Instagram post, and its bankruptcy trustee says another $1.2 million went to a modeling agency. You needed real money to sell a fake paradise.

That price tag kept most small-time scammers out. Now the picture costs about nothing, and regulators still show up weeks after the doors open, one complaint at a time.

So expect a few more of these every December. If a holiday event looks perfect online and you can't find one real photo of the actual place, you probably already know what's inside.

A Christmas market in England advertised itself with an AI picture of a cozy wooden lodge, fairy lights everywhere, and a stage set up for a band. One vendor paid £180 for a stall.

Opening day was a concrete warehouse with about five stalls and a red bucket on the floor catching rain from the roof.

Entry was free, so the money came from vendors like her. And the way they got pulled in is kind of clever.

Think about how a new market gets off the ground. Vendors won't pay for a spot unless they believe crowds are coming, and crowds won't come unless there are vendors worth seeing. Every market has to break that loop somehow, and the honest way takes years of showing up and building a reputation.

This one used a picture. The same image went out to vendors and shoppers, and each side looked at it and saw the other side already there. Vendors say they were promised 50-plus stalls and 2,500-plus visitors a day.

The guy who made the images, David Rowland, runs the bigger Winter Wonderland attraction next door. He called it a "lesson learned" and said you're never going to get it looking exactly like the picture. The organizers have since cancelled every booking and promised full refunds.

outsiders.name: Aakash Gupta
outsiders.text:
A Christmas market in England advertised itself with an AI picture of a cozy wooden lodge, fairy lights everywhere, and a stage set up for a band. One vendor paid £180 for a stall.

Opening day was a concrete warehouse with about five stalls and a red bucket on the floor catching rain from the roof.

Entry was free, so the money came from vendors like her. And the way they got pulled in is kind of clever.

Think about how a new market gets off the ground. Vendors won't pay for a spot unless they believe crowds are coming, and crowds won't come unless there are vendors worth seeing. Every market has to break that loop somehow, and the honest way takes years of showing up and building a reputation.

This one used a picture. The same image went out to vendors and shoppers, and each side looked at it and saw the other side already there. Vendors say they were promised 50-plus stalls and 2,500-plus visitors a day.

The guy who made the images, David Rowland, runs the bigger Winter Wonderland attraction next door. He called it a "lesson learned" and said you're never going to get it looking exactly like the picture. The organizers have since cancelled every booking and promised full refunds.

Glasgow pulled the same move in February 2024. Willy's Chocolate Experience sold £35 tickets off AI posters so sloppy they had made-up words on them, families walked into a mostly empty warehouse, and somebody called the cops. Nearly three years later, the pictures look a whole lot more real.

So is this legal? Nope, and it hasn't been for a long time. Britain passed the Trade Descriptions Act back in 1968. The UK ad watchdog says AI images get judged the same as photos. And since April 2025, the competition regulator can fine a company up to 10% of its global revenue without even going to court. One vendor is already talking to lawyers.

Faking a place used to be expensive, though. Fyre Festival paid Kendall Jenner $250,000 for one Instagram post, and its bankruptcy trustee says another $1.2 million went to a modeling agency. You needed real money to sell a fake paradise.

That price tag kept most small-time scammers out. Now the picture costs about nothing, and regulators still show up weeks after the doors open, one complaint at a time.

So expect a few more of these every December. If a holiday event looks perfect online and you can't find one real photo of the actual place, you probably already know what's inside.
